sessions.title: Distinguish changed meanings and genuine aspect partners

steps.title: Different prefixes can change the meaning
steps.body: отговорить — to dissuade. договориться — to agree. These are different meanings, even though the words share material with a verb of speaking. A prefix is not always just an aspect marker: learn the whole verb and its meaning.

steps.title: The actual dissuade aspect pair
steps.body: отговаривать is the imperfective partner of perfective отговорить: both concern dissuading. The retained source explicitly identifies this pair. сказать belongs to a separate speaking pair; it is not the imperfective partner of отговорить. For a question asking for the perfective partner of отговаривать, select отговорить. договориться is a different verb meaning to agree.

steps.title: Keep the other meanings separate
steps.body: написать — to write. сделать — to do. Neither expresses dissuading or agreeing. When a question asks for a meaning, translate the displayed verb. When it asks for an aspect partner, preserve the lexical meaning while changing aspect. These selections do not demonstrate creating new prefixed verbs or using aspect in a sentence.

sessions.title: Interpret conditional structure and speaker agreement

steps.title: The past form with a conditional particle
steps.body: я спал бы is used by a male speaker; я спала́ бы is used by a female speaker. These labels describe the speaker marked by the past-form agreement; they are not translations of the whole expressions. Both use the first-person pronoun, a past-form verb and the conditional particle. In this construction the past form need not report an actual past event: it can express a hypothetical situation, such as I would sleep. Context supplies the time reference.

steps.title: Read agreement rather than an English sentence label
steps.body: Compare the two retained forms я спал бы and я спала́ бы. The feminine past form has a final vowel that the masculine form lacks. For the first choose a male speaker; for the second choose a female speaker. I would like to sleep is a sentence meaning, not a label identifying the gender marked by the shown past form. Speaker agreement and sentence meaning are different questions.

steps.title: A wish and a different position for the particle
steps.body: я бы поспа́л — I would like to sleep. я бы поспала́ has feminine speaker agreement: the speaker is marked feminine. The first-person pronoun identifies the speaker, rather than another person. These retained wish expressions have the conditional particle before the verb, whereas the earlier examples put it after the verb. It cannot begin its clause. The wish reading comes from the construction and context, not from translating every conditional particle as would like. These choices do not demonstrate independently forming a conditional sentence or an aspect choice.

steps.title: An obligation for a masculine speaker
steps.body: я должен — I have to. This retained phrase expresses obligation for a masculine singular speaker. The short adjective agrees with the subject, and an infinitive can name the required action. The subject is nominative. The shown phrase does not name an action, so do not infer a particular task from it.

steps.title: Feminine, neuter and plural agreement
steps.body: должна — If the subject is feminine. должно — If the subject is neuter. должны — If the subject is plural. These retained English labels describe agreement; they are not literal translations of each Russian word. Select the feminine label for the feminine form and the plural label for the plural form. The short adjective changes with the subject, while the infinitive naming the action does not acquire a gender ending.

steps.title: Separate an agreement label from a meaning
steps.body: I have to is the meaning of the retained first-person phrase. If the subject is feminine and If the subject is plural are labels describing which form to use. A question asking for an agreement label differs from one asking what the whole phrase means. Obligation is one use of this adjective; an expected-event reading is taught separately. These selections do not demonstrate independently producing an obligation statement or using all tense forms.

steps.title: An expected eclipse
steps.body: Затме́ние должно́ наступи́ть в три часа́. — The eclipse should occur at three o'clock. Here should expresses an expected event, not a duty imposed on the eclipse. The short adjective agrees with the neuter subject and the infinitive names the event. The retained usage description is (with a verb) Used to express likelihood. Usually translated as "should".

steps.title: An employee obligation
steps.body: Слу́жащие должны́ во́время явля́ться на рабо́ту. — Employees must report to work on time. This states an obligation for plural employees. The English label an obligation describes a required action; an expected event describes a prediction such as the eclipse. Context determines which sense the shared adjective-plus-infinitive structure expresses. One independent check asks for the eclipse sentence meaning; the other classifies the employee obligation. These two examples do not demonstrate independent sentence production or every use of the adjective.

objectives.title: Distinguish motion meaning, directionality and setting out

steps.title: Admitted motion lines

sessions.title: Distinguish motion meaning, directionality and setting out

steps.title: Walking and travelling by vehicle
steps.body: идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

steps.title: Directionality is separate from aspect
steps.body: The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

steps.title: Carrying, leading and transporting
steps.body: нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

steps.title: Setting out does not assert arrival
steps.body: Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

steps.title: Read the path and only the displayed clause
steps.body: Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они у́летят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

steps.title: Interpret directionality in a whole example
steps.body: Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

steps.title: Distinguish repeated trips and a completed return
steps.body: Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the retained supplied context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). The past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. A choice saying “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” makes an incorrect aspect inference for these forms. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.

objectives.title: Connect own possession to the subject and the possessed noun
Distinguish oneself from a possessed object
Distinguish purpose, condition, cause and concession

steps.title: Admitted object and purpose lines
steps.body: Proposed Unit 21 uses frozen object-possession lines, the frozen reflexive contrast, and the frozen purpose gloss. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 21 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

sessions.title: Connect own possession to the subject and the possessed noun

steps.title: Who owns it and which noun controls the form
steps.body: The reflexive possessive refers to the subject as the owner. Its gender, number and case agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner. The retained dictionary forms are свой, своя, своё and свои. A masculine owner and a feminine owner can therefore use the same possessive form with the same noun.

steps.title: The movie belongs to the subject
steps.body: Бо́ря рассказа́л о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Borya told about his favorite movie.). А́нна рассказа́ла о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Anna told about her favorite movie.). In each sentence the favorite movie belongs to the subject. The movie noun has the same gender, number and case in both, so the possessive form stays the same. The name and past-verb agreement change. The exercise asks you to preserve that movie object while changing the subject.

steps.title: The same own book with two subjects
steps.body: Свое́й кни́ги она́ никогда́ не написа́ла. — (She never wrote her own book.). Свое́й кни́ги он никогда́ не написа́л. — (He never wrote his own book.). The possessive agrees with the feminine singular book noun; the shown form is genitive in this negative sentence. Changing the subject changes the past verb's agreement, not the book phrase. These sentences are about a book, not a movie or jeans.

steps.title: Plural jeans and the limits of the checks
steps.body: Бо́ря наде́л свои́ джи́нсы. — (Borya put on his own jeans.). А́нна наде́ла свои́ джи́нсы. — (Anna put on her own jeans.). Plural jeans require plural possessive agreement regardless of whether Borya or Anna owns them. The exercise keeps this object and changes the subject. The checks select supplied matched sentences; they do not demonstrate independently declining the possessive or constructing an ownership sentence.

steps.title: Review the complete contrast
steps.body:
The reflexive possessive refers to the subject as the owner. Its gender, number and case agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner. The retained dictionary forms are свой, своя, своё and свои. A masculine owner and a feminine owner can therefore use the same possessive form with the same noun.

Бо́ря рассказа́л о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Borya told about his favorite movie.). А́нна рассказа́ла о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Anna told about her favorite movie.). In each sentence the favorite movie belongs to the subject. The movie noun has the same gender, number and case in both, so the possessive form stays the same. The name and past-verb agreement change. The exercise asks you to preserve that movie object while changing the subject.

Свое́й кни́ги она́ никогда́ не написа́ла. — (She never wrote her own book.). Свое́й кни́ги он никогда́ не написа́л. — (He never wrote his own book.). The possessive agrees with the feminine singular book noun; the shown form is genitive in this negative sentence. Changing the subject changes the past verb's agreement, not the book phrase. These sentences are about a book, not a movie or jeans.

Бо́ря наде́л свои́ джи́нсы. — (Borya put on his own jeans.). А́нна наде́ла свои́ джи́нсы. — (Anna put on her own jeans.). Plural jeans require plural possessive agreement regardless of whether Borya or Anna owns them. The exercise keeps this object and changes the subject. The checks select supplied matched sentences; they do not demonstrate independently declining the possessive or constructing an ownership sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish oneself from a possessed object

steps.title: The person loved and the person who owns
steps.body: Я люблю́ себя́ — I love myself. Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ — I love my wife. In the first sentence the object refers back to the subject. In the second the object is a wife; the parenthesized possessive makes ownership explicit. Loving oneself and loving a wife describe different objects.

steps.title: A whole sentence is more than its object word
steps.body: жену́ is the accusative form of the noun meaning wife. It does not mean I love. In Я люблю́ свою́ жену́ the verb supplies loving and the noun supplies its object. The full displayed sentence Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ means I love my wife; the full displayed sentence Я люблю́ себя́ means I love myself. Choose the whole-sentence meaning rather than translating the object word as the verb. These checks recognize the supplied love and wounded-object sentences; they do not demonstrate independently choosing every reflexive case form.

steps.title: Recognize the same-person object in a different sentence
steps.body: Он поранил себя — He has wounded himself. Here the subject denotes the man and the direct object себя refers back to that same person. The verb and subject differ from guided Я люблю́ себя́. Compare the complete supplied Он поранил его — He has wounded him (someone else). In this contrast the other person is the object; the person wounded is different from the subject. In both wounded sentences the object is a person, not a possessed wife. In the retained Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ example, a wife is the object even when the possessive refers to the subject as owner. Keep object identity separate from ownership. These are supplied direct-object readings, not productive grammar, every pronoun case, emphasis or a rule that the reflexive-verb suffix always means accidental action.

sessions.title: Distinguish purpose, condition, cause and concession

steps.title: Purpose and condition
steps.body: чтобы — so that. если — if. The first conjunction can introduce a purpose; the second introduces a condition. In a purpose construction with the same subject for both actions, an infinitive after the purpose conjunction can name the intended action. This rule is explained here, but the current choices do not require composing such a sentence.

steps.title: Ordinary purpose wording
steps.body: чтобы is an ordinary purpose conjunction. The bookish or archaic qualifier in the retained source belongs to дабы, not to чтобы. The English meaning so that differs from the conditional if and the causal because. Select the meaning of the displayed conjunction; do not infer an archaic register for the ordinary form.

steps.title: Cause, concession and time
steps.body: потому что — because. хотя — although. The first gives a reason; the second introduces a concession. The English label after names a temporal relationship rather than a reason. English since can also express a reason, so it is not a contrasting wrong answer to because in this exercise. The causal check instead contrasts because with although and after. These conjunction meanings are distinct from purpose and condition.
